pageTitle: Guitar Picks: Material Science, Bevel Geometry & Kinetic Transfer
subtitle: Master pick gauges, materials from Delrin to Vespel, bevel angles, attack physics, and tone shaping

introduction.title: The Guitar Pick: The Primary Acoustic Interface
introduction.text: The plectrum is the very first physical point of contact in the sound production chain. Long before a vibration reaches tonewoods, magnetic pickups, preamps, or tube amplifiers, the pick excites the string. A guitar pick is a precision acoustic tool: its chemical polymer composition governs friction and scratch noise; its tip radius and edge bevel dictate the release trajectory of the vibrating string; and its gauge dictates kinetic energy transfer. Swapping from a flexible 0.50 mm nylon pick to a rigid 1.5 mm Ultex Jazz III alters the frequency spectrum, harmonic attack transient, and dynamic headroom more drastically than changing guitar cables or tubes.
introduction.quote: The pick is the needle on the record of your guitar; its material, bevel, and mass sculpt the raw harmonic signature of every note.

columns.title: Kinetic Energy Transfer & Diaphragm Mass
columns.text: When a plectrum strikes a tensioned guitar string, it displaces the string laterally until the restoring mechanical tension overcomes the frictional coefficient between pick and metal. A flexible thin pick ($< 0.60\text{ mm}$) absorbs kinetic energy by bending, releasing the string with low kinetic momentum. This acts as an acoustic compressor—ideal for even acoustic strumming. A rigid heavy pick ($> 1.0\text{ mm}$) does not bend, transferring 100% of muscular kinetic energy directly into the string core, producing a massive fundamental transient, increased acoustic volume, and instantaneous dynamic touch response.

columns.title: The Physics of Edge Bevels & Attack Angle
columns.text: As a pick travels through a string, edge geometry governs resistance. A square, blunt edge catches the string, causing mechanical drag and microphonic 'chirp'. A hand-polished 45-degree 'speed bevel' creates a ramp that allows the string to glide effortlessly off the tip. Striking the string flat (parallel) produces maximum fundamental punch, while angling the pick 20 to 30 degrees (slicing) minimizes string contact time, exciting bright upper partials and unlocking blistering alternate picking speeds.

cards.title: Celluloid vs Delrin (Tortex) vs Nylon
cards.description: The foundational polymers of modern guitar playing.

fields.label: Celluloid (Traditional)
fields.value: Originally developed as a synthetic substitute for endangered tortoiseshell. Offers balanced flexibility, smooth string release, and a warm, organic click on acoustic and vintage electric setups.

fields.label: Delrin / Tortex (Dunlop)
fields.value: Engineered acetal polymer with a matte, chalky surface that absorbs fingertip moisture. Highly resistant to edge wear with a crisp, aggressive snap favored in rock, metal, and pop.

fields.label: Nylon (Molded Grip)
fields.value: Soft, ductile polymer with high impact resistance. Yields a smooth, warm attack that dampens high-frequency string scratch, featuring raised tactile grip patterns for high-sweat live environments.

cards.title: Engineering Polymers: Ultex vs Acrylic vs Vespel
cards.description: High-performance aerospace and industrial plastics designed for speed and longevity.

fields.label: Ultex / Ultem (Polyetherimide)
fields.value: Aerospace polymer with an exceptional stiffness-to-weight ratio. Produces a bright, glassy acoustic chirp, massive dynamic headroom, and virtually zero wear across months of heavy playing.

fields.label: Cast Acrylic (V-Picks, Gravity)
fields.value: Thick, crystal-clear acrylic that warms to body temperature and clings to the fingers. Glides across strings with zero drag, delivering huge low-end fundamental weight.

fields.label: Vespel SP-1 Polyimide (BlueChip)
fields.value: Ultra-expensive aerospace thermoset plastic ($35+ per pick). Self-lubricating, virtually indestructible, and completely free of pick click, representing the absolute holy grail of bluegrass and acoustic tone.

cards.title: Grip Pressure & The Slicing Angle
cards.description: Right-hand grip tension directly governs dynamic range and speed.

fields.label: The Loose Grip Paradox
fields.value: Grip the pick just firmly enough so it does not rotate, but loose enough that it flexes minutely between thumb and index. Squeezing too hard introduces forearm tension that throttles speed and produces harsh, thin tone.

fields.label: The 30-Degree Slicing Attack
fields.value: Angle the pick edge approximately 30 degrees to the string rather than slapping flat. Slicing glides across the string with minimal resistance, dramatically accelerating alternate picking runs.

fields.label: Choking Down for Pinch Harmonics
fields.value: Expose only 2 to 3 mm of the pick tip. When striking the string, allow the fleshy edge of the right thumb to brush the vibrating string simultaneously, exciting piercing artificial harmonics.

cards.title: Wear Patterns & Custom Edge Polishing
cards.description: A pick's edge wears down rapidly from friction against wound strings.

fields.label: The Serration Danger
fields.value: Wound steel strings grind jagged micro-grooves into plastic pick edges. These microscopic burs catch on strings, causing harsh scratching noises and broken high E strings.

fields.label: Emery & Leather Polishing
fields.value: Restore worn pick bevels by buffing them against 1,000-grit sandpaper followed by a swipe across a leather strap or denim jeans to restore a glass-smooth release.

fields.label: When to Retire
fields.value: When a pick's tip has rounded off significantly, throwing off your picking depth perception, discard it. Picks are cheap consumables—never compromise technique for a worn $0.50 pick.
